description: We’re a team of curious minds, creative thinkers, and passionate problem-solvers ready to explore the unknown! Our mission is to bring Mars a little closer to Earth through innovative mapping, scientific discovery, and technology. Whether you’re passionate about astronomy, coding, design, research, or simply exploring the mysteries of the universe, we believe every perspective can make a difference. Together, we’re not just mapping Mars — we’re charting the future of exploration!
summary:
We developed a Mars surface-exploration system with three parts. A scout drone flies ahead as the astronaut's GPS, matching its camera view to NASA's HiRISE orbital images. A dock uses zeolite sponges to pull CO₂ from the Martian air to refill the drone's canisters. An AR display inside the helmet shows the safe route, hazards, oxygen, radiation and the way home. Electrodynamic dust shields keep the visor, cameras and solar panels clear. We built an interactive simulator at Gale Crater using real NASA elevation data.

It answers the challenge by layering five NASA data types: images, elevation, radiation, weather and pressure, and dust storms. These produce a route that avoids obstacles and puts safety first. The point-of-no-return alert, radiation shelters and a step-tracking fallback bring the astronaut home even if the drone fails.

It matters because Mars has no GPS and Earth is up to 24 minutes away by radio. Astronauts need to know where they are and what's ahead without waiting for help.
details:
We designed the Mars Scout Drone to help astronauts navigate Mars safely without GPS. A drone flies ahead to scout hazards like rocks, steep slopes, and loose sand. An augmented reality visor shows the suggested route in cyan, marks hazards in red, and uses the astronaut’s remaining oxygen and distance from base to recommend when to turn back.

Our design accounts for dust storms, limited sunlight, and drone failure. Electric fields help keep dust off the visor and cameras, while a solar-powered dock captures CO₂ from Martian air to refill the drone’s canisters. If a storm forces the drone to return, the visor can guide the astronaut home using a trail of recorded positions.

We used real NASA elevation data from Gale Crater to build an interactive simulator where users can switch between astronaut and drone views and trigger a dust storm. By combining aerial scouting, hands-free guidance, and resources already available on Mars, our project aims to make surface exploration safer and give astronauts more time for scientific work.
